claims.text: THE NAMING DISCREPANCY, STATED RATHER THAN RESOLVED. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log for 10 November 1975 reads: 'UFO sighting reported by Minot Air Force Station, a bright star-like object in the West, moving east, about the size of a car. First seen approximately 1015Z. Approximately 1120Z the object passed over the radar station, 1,000 feet to 2,000 feet high, no noise heard. Three people from the site or local area saw the object.' The CINCNORAD four-part message of 11 November 1975 instead lists 'Minot AFB, ND'. Minot Air Force Station is a radar site and is not the 91st Strategic Missile Wing's missile field. No opened record resolves which installation the 1975 sequence means.

claims.text: The 24 October 1968 case generated a dense primary file: Project Blue Book's final case report of 13 November 1968, twelve pages; Basic Reporting Data of 28 October 1968, eight pages, prepared by Lt Col Arthur J. Werlich of the 862nd Combat Support Group Operations Division; the 91st Strategic Missile Wing Security Controller's summary listing UFO observers at Launch Control Facilities with sighting times; the Base Operations Dispatcher's Log for 0800 to 1010Z recording ground reports from site N-7; seven AF Form 117 witness questionnaires; thirteen B-52 ASQ-38 radarscope photographs with data plates; the Werlich overlay map at 1:200,000; and a transcription of recorded conversations between the B-52 co-pilot and Radar Approach Control.

Seven airmen completed AF Form 117 questionnaires in 1968, which places their statements in the contemporaneous official record rather than in any later interview: A1C Lloyd M. Isley and A1C Robert Michael O'Connor of the 91st MIMS; A1C Joseph Patrick Jablonski, A1C Gregory Adams, SSgt James Frederick Bond and SSgt William E. Smith Jr. of the 862nd SPS; and Major James A. Partin, pilot, 23rd Bomb Squadron, 5th Bomb Wing.

Minot is named in the CINCNORAD four-part message of 11 November 1975: 'Since 28 Oct 75 numerous reports of suspicious objects have been received at the NORAD CU; reliable military personnel at Loring AFB, Maine, Wurtsmith AFB, Michigan, Malmstrom AFB, Mt, Minot AFB, ND, and Canadian Forces Station, Falconbridge, Ontario, Canada have visually sighted suspicious objects.'

desc: THE HUB WITH THE MOST INDEPENDENT DETECTION CHANNELS AND ONE UNRESOLVED NAMING PROBLEM. Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota, home of the 91st Strategic Missile Wing and the 5th Bomb Wing, is the convergence point for three separate episodes this board already carries in pieces without a place to hang them on: the 1966 incursions over its Minuteman launch facilities, the 24 October 1968 B-52 case, which is the best-instrumented nuclear-site incursion in the American record, and its named appearance in the CINCNORAD four-part message of 11 November 1975. THE NAMING PROBLEM IS REAL AND MUST NOT BE SILENTLY RESOLVED. For 10 November 1975 the 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log records a sighting at 'Minot Air Force Station', a radar site, and its own next clause says the object 'passed over the radar station'. Nine days later CINCNORAD's summary message lists 'Minot AFB, ND' among the installations where reliable military personnel had visually sighted suspicious objects. Two NORAD documents from the same period name two different Minot installations, and nothing opened by this board resolves which is meant. That matters for this hub specifically, because a degree count on l-minot that silently absorbs a radar-station entry is a degree count that lies.
